newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's ruling party vows crackdown on vote-buying.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's ruling party vows crackdown on vote-buying.

text.p: South Korea's ruling party, embroiled in new allegations of corruption, on Tuesday vowed to deal sternly with any vote-buying during elections for the party's presidential nominee.
New Korea Party's acting chairman Lee Man-sup's comments followed allegations on Monday that the party's top candidate had paid off delegates who will vote in the elections.
The candidate, Lee Hoi-chang, a former judge and one-time premier nicknamed "Mr Clean", has denied the accusations made by one of his opponents in the seven-person race, Park Chan-jong.
"If there is any evidence of vote-buying among the candidates, they will be disqualified from the race, and even after a nominee is elected he will be expelled," Lee Man-sup told a news conference.
The acting chairman stressed that Park had produced no evidence to back up his allegations.
"A successful nomination race will enhance democracy in Korea and help our party win the public's trust," said Lee.
A party official, who declined to be identified, said the affair had hurt Lee Hoi-chang.
"Our party must reveal the full truth to prevent any further damage to our top candidate," he said.

Park has said he will submit evidence of vote-buying directly to President Kim Young-sam, the party president, to prevent any tampering. Lee Hoi-chang has threatened to file for defamation if no evidence is offered.
The New Korea Party will elect its candidate on July 21 after the first ever open race for a presidential nominee by the country's ruling party.

The two main opposition parties have already elected their candidates for presidential polls in December. The constitution bars current head of state Kim Young-sam from seeking a second term in office.
Lee said at a news conference on Tuesday that he was confident a clean race would help improve the party's image already battered by a string of corruption scandals.
Several senior party figures are serving long jail terms for taking kickbacks from the Hanbo Group, whose steelmaking flagship collapsed under large debts in January, revealing a web of corruption.
Political analysts said mud-slinging within the New Korea Party was unlikely to hurt the party in December elections.

"Without any evidence, the accusations won't hurt Lee Hoi-chang at the party race and by December the public won't even remember the allegations," said Yonsei University political science professor Shin Myung-soon.
"The ruling party's main worry is one of the 'dragons' leaving the group to run alone, splitting the votes," said Shim, referring to ruling party hopefuls, dubbed "dragons".
Shim said Lee Hoi-chang may decide to run as an independent if he is not elected on Monday. Opinion polls indicate Lee Hoi-chang is the most popular candidate.
Political analysts said a split ruling party ticket would give the opposition a chance of victory in December.
The two opposition leaders, Kim Dae-jung and Kim Jong-pil, are now negotiating on a single candidacy.

The other five ruling party "dragons" are President Kim's long-time supporter, Kim Deog-ryong, former prosecutor-turned-lawmaker, Lee Han-dong, former Seoul mayor, Choe Byung-yul, legal scholar Lee Soo-sung and Rhee In-je, governor of Kyonggi Province.
